title: Letter IV
focus: the meeting of two ambitious men

teacherSummary.text: Trapped in ice, Walton's crew sees a giant figure on a dog sled, and the next morning rescues a frozen, exhausted stranger: Victor Frankenstein. Victor recovers slowly, becomes Walton's friend, and, hearing of Walton's ambition, agrees to tell his own story as a warning.

vocabulary.definition: To settle or draw up the heads or terms of an agreement, as in chapters or articles
vocabulary.context: Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “capitulate”: cap (Latin capere, "to take") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: One who guards, protects, watches over, or has the care of, some person or thing
vocabulary.context: You have been tutored and refined by books and retirement from the world, and you are, therefore, somewhat fastidious; but this only renders you the more fit to appreciate the extraordinary merits of this wonderful man.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tutor”: -or (Latin -or, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An optical instrument used in viewing distant objects, as the heavenly bodies
vocabulary.context: We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes, until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “telescope”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being raw
vocabulary.context: He manifested the greatest eagerness to be upon deck, to watch for the sledge which had before appeared; but I have persuaded him to remain in the cabin, for he is far too weak to sustain the rawness of the atmosphere.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “rawness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Coming or happening as a consequence or result
vocabulary.context: He entered attentively into all my arguments in favour of my eventual success, and into every minute detail of the measures I had taken to secure it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “eventual”: vent (Latin venire, "to come") + -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To throw rays of light upon
vocabulary.context: Even now, as I commence my task, his full-toned voice swells in my ears; his lustrous eyes dwell on me with all their melancholy sweetness; I see his thin hand raised in animation, while the lineaments of his face are irradiated by the soul within.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “irradiate”: ir- (Latin in-, "not") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Having a disposition to do good
vocabulary.context: “And yet you rescued me from a strange and perilous situation; you have benevolently restored me to life.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “benevolent”: bene- (Latin bene, "well") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Yet his manners are so conciliating and gentle, that the sailors are all interested in him, although they have had very little communication with him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conciliate”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: But he is generally melancholy and despairing; and sometimes he gnashes his teeth, as if impatient of the weight of woes that oppresses him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “oppress”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To flow in a small, gentle stream
vocabulary.context: At first I perceived that he tried to suppress his emotion; he placed his hands before his eyes; and my voice quivered and failed me, as I beheld tears trickle fast from between his fingers—a groan burst from his heaving breast.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “trickle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: The frame (Walton) now opens into Victor's narrative, a 'story within a story' structure called a nested or frame narrative.

significance: Victor's warning, 'Learn from me,' makes the whole novel a cautionary tale addressed to Walton and to the reader.
discussionQuestions: Victor says he will tell his story so Walton may learn from it. What lesson do you predict?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Letter IV,” how does Shelley show the meeting of two ambitious men? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Letter IV, how does Shelley develop the idea of the meeting of two ambitious men? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Letter IV develops the idea of the meeting of two ambitious men. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Letter IV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of the meeting of two ambitious men. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Letter IV suggests about the meeting of two ambitious men. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Letter IV to complicate the reader's understanding of the meeting of two ambitious men. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Letter IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the meeting of two ambitious men responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Letter IV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the meeting of two ambitious men follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Letter IV and its treatment of the meeting of two ambitious men. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Letter IV as evidence for a larger claim about the meeting of two ambitious men in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Letter IV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the meeting of two ambitious men. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes, until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.
satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “telescopes” most nearly mean?
options: An optical instrument used in viewing distant objects, as the heavenly bodies
To flow in a small, gentle stream

satQuestions.passage: About two o’clock the mist cleared away, and we beheld, stretched out in every direction, vast and irregular plains of ice, which seemed to have no end. Some of my comrades groaned, and my own mind began to grow watchful with anxious thoughts, when a strange sight suddenly attracted our attention, and diverted our solicitude from our own situation. We perceived a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and drawn by dogs, pass on towards the north, at the distance of half a mile: a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge, and guided the dogs. We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes, until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Letter IV”?
options: The meeting of two ambitious men

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Victor says he will tell his story so Walton may learn from it. What lesson do you predict? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are capitulated, tutored, telescopes, rawness, eventual. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless.” Webster's says: To settle or draw up the heads or terms of an agreement, as in chapters or articles. Now the word history: “capitulate”: cap (Latin capere, "to take") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “tutor”: -or (Latin -or, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “telescope”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The frame (Walton) now opens into Victor's narrative, a 'story within a story' structure called a nested or frame narrative. Why does this chapter matter? Victor's warning, 'Learn from me,' makes the whole novel a cautionary tale addressed to Walton and to the reader. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the meeting of two ambitious men.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Point of view.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: About two o’clock the mist cleared away, and we beheld, stretched out in every direction, vast and irregular plains of ice, which seemed to have no end. Some of my comrades groaned, and my own mind began to grow watchful with anxious thoughts, when a strange sight suddenly attracted our attention, and diverted our solicitude from our own situation. We perceived a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and drawn by dogs, pass on towards the north, at the distance of half a mile: a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge, and guided the dogs. We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes, until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Point of view: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Letter IV,” how does Shelley show the meeting of two ambitious men? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the meeting of two ambitious men, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes the meeting of two ambitious men. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
